title: Invariance Audits for Quantum Kernels and Variational Rewinding: A Real-to-Hermitian Taxonomy of Projector, Flag, Anchor, and Density Geometry
authors: Azadeh Alavi, Fatemeh Kouchmeshki, Hossein Akhoundi
abstract: Machine-learning models often replace vectors by normalized directions, projectors, covariances, subspaces, ordered flags, quantum states, or density operators before any classifier is fitted. This replacement is an invariance decision: it determines which distinctions are kept and which are quotiented out. We develop a self-contained real-to-Hermitian taxonomy for auditing such representations in quantum machine learning. On the real side, we formalize Grassmann and flag projector kernels, prove positive semidefiniteness and block-gauge invariance of a weighted flag kernel, and give a same-span block-swap witness showing when whole-span Grassmann geometry must fail while ordered flags succeed. On the quantum side, we prove that a noiseless fidelity kernel is exactly the Hilbert--Schmidt inner product between the associated rank-one Hermitian projectors, and that a QVR-style return probability is exactly an overlap score between the input projector and a learned anchor operator. Rank-constrained returns correspond to complex Grassmann anchors, while mixed or multimodal class models are naturally represented by density or positive-semidefinite anchors. Controlled vector, subspace, statevector, anomaly, finite-shot, and quotient-witness experiments support the same conclusion: quantum and geometric lifts are useful when their invariances match the task, and fail correctly when discarded information is label-bearing. The paper makes no hardware-speedup or quantum-advantage claim.
summary: This paper creates a formal taxonomy to audit the geometric assumptions made when using quantum representations (like projectors or subspaces) in machine learning. It proves that various complex quantum scoring methods are mathematically equivalent to simpler, traceable Hermitian projector overlaps. The work emphasizes that the utility of any quantum ML approach depends entirely on whether its inherent mathematical invariances match the physical symmetries of the problem being solved.
main_problem: The paper addresses how machine learning models implicitly make 'invariance decisions' when replacing raw data vectors with geometric representations like projectors, subspaces, or density operators.
main_result: It develops a formal taxonomy showing that the choice of representation dictates the imposed invariance, proving key equivalences between quantum fidelity kernels and Hermitian projector traces.
method: The authors develop a mathematical framework—a 'real-to-Hermitian taxonomy'—to audit these geometric lifts by comparing kernel methods (Grassmann/Flag) against variational return probability scoring mechanisms.
model_or_system: The focus is on Quantum Machine Learning (QML) representations, analyzing geometries such as the Grassmannian manifold and complex projective space ($\mathbb{CP}^{D-1}$) using projectors ($P$), density operators ($ho$), and learned anchor matrices ($A_	heta$).
key_observables: Invariance properties (e.g., block-gauge invariance), kernel values, QVR return probabilities ($p_	heta(x)$), and trace consistency between different scoring methods.
important_parameters: The dimensionality of the Hilbert space ($D$), the rank of projectors ($r$), and the number of measurement shots/noise levels are key parameters in the audits.
main_assumptions: The paper explicitly states it makes no claim regarding hardware speedup or quantum advantage; all results are derived from statevector simulations using controlled, synthetic datasets as witnesses.
figures_summary: Tables summarize comparisons across various ML tasks (e.g., classwise anchor protocols, regression performance) and provide conceptual mappings between different geometric representations and their associated invariances.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the core problem of invariance decisions to developing mathematical proofs for specific kernels (Grassmann/Flag), establishing equivalences (Fidelity $\leftrightarrow$ Projector Trace), and concluding with a comprehensive taxonomy supported by multiple comparative audits.
why_interesting: While not directly about AMO dynamics, the rigorous geometric analysis of quantum information structures (projectors, density matrices) provides deep mathematical tools for understanding how physical constraints manifest as computational invariances in QML applications.
